Explain causes and assess consequences for the Greek world. Political and military aspects are expressly required.

aspects.name: Political

facts.claim: Herodotus attributes Xerxes’ invasion to imperial expansion and retaliation for Athenian intervention at Sardis and the earlier defeat.
Thucydides describes the victorious coalition subsequently dividing into Athenian and Spartan alliance systems.

aspects.causal_explanation: Evaluator inference: Connect Persian domination and intervention to conflict; explain how successful collective defence could preserve autonomy yet redistribute power and generate rivalry.

aspects.name: Military

facts.claim: Athens supplied 180 ships at Salamis; the allied fleet was formally commanded by the Spartan Eurybiades.
Pausanias led the Spartan expedition against the remaining Persian forces in the Plataea campaign.

aspects.causal_explanation: Evaluator inference: Explain complementary naval and land operations rather than listing victories; victory depended on coalition resources and did not abolish later warfare.

traps.claim_or_issue: All Greek states fought as a single united nation.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Coalition membership and later alignments varied; Greek unity was partial and temporary.

traps.claim_or_issue: A purely moral freedom-versus-tyranny explanation establishes Persian motives.
traps.correction_or_caveat: This may frame a Greek perspective, but expansion and retaliation need concrete treatment; Herodotus’ speeches are literary representations.

topics.interpretive_flexibility: Accept different balances of autonomy, Athenian ascendancy, coalition achievement and ensuing rivalry if both required aspects and a causal assessment are supported.

requirements: Choose one alternative; state and justify a position with historical evidence; requested length 400–500 words.

Compare Athens and Sparta in the defence of Hellas. The dimensions below organize research; the prompt names no separate compulsory scoring aspects.

aspects.name: Research dimension: Athenian contribution

facts.claim: Thucydides connects Themistocles’ fleet-building policy to the ships used at Salamis.
The Athenian contingent of 180 ships was the largest at Salamis.

aspects.causal_explanation: Evaluator inference: Relate investment and naval capacity to resisting invasion; strategic influence can be assessed without equating it with formal supreme command.

aspects.name: Research dimension: Spartan leadership and coalition

facts.claim: Eurybiades held allied naval command after Athens conceded leadership to maintain cooperation.
Spartan regent Pausanias commanded the expedition in the Plataea campaign.

aspects.causal_explanation: Evaluator inference: Different military strengths and accepted leadership helped coordination; other allied contingents also mattered.

traps.claim_or_issue: Themistocles was the formal commander of every Greek naval force.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Distinguish Athenian strategic leadership from Eurybiades’ formal command.

traps.claim_or_issue: Athens alone defeated Persia, or Sparta contributed only at Thermopylae.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Assess both cities and coalition contributions rather than excluding one through a single-battle account.

topics.interpretive_flexibility: A reasoned ranking or a complementary-contribution argument is acceptable; no exact ranking or mandatory battle inventory is imposed.

Characterize the Republican constitution and assess its effectiveness. Constitutional and social aspects are expressly required.

aspects.name: Constitutional

facts.claim: Polybius distinguishes consuls, Senate and people; the Senate controls finance while popular bodies elect officials and decide laws and war or peace.
Tribunician intervention could block Senate action; consuls depended on funds and public approval.

aspects.causal_explanation: Evaluator inference: Assess whether divided authority and dependencies restrained power and enabled government, while considering their vulnerability to obstruction.

aspects.name: Social

facts.claim: Appian links concentration of public land and slave cultivation to pressure on free farmers; Tiberius Gracchus proposed redistribution.
Octavius vetoed the agrarian measure; his removal and Tiberius’ killing illustrate institutional conflict escalating into violence.

aspects.causal_explanation: Evaluator inference: Connect representation and veto to conflicting social interests; assess practical responsiveness rather than treating institutional design as equal participation for all.

traps.claim_or_issue: The Senate was a modern elected parliament or the Republic a universal democracy.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Characterize actual Roman bodies and powers rather than importing modern institutions.

traps.claim_or_issue: Institutional effectiveness was uniformly high or uniformly absent throughout the Republic.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Time, task and social perspective matter; a qualified assessment can weigh stable cooperation against crisis.

topics.interpretive_flexibility: Accept an argument emphasizing successful expansion, institutional balance, elite dominance, or eventual dysfunction if grounded and responsive to both aspects.

requirements: Choose one alternative; state and justify a position with historical evidence; requested length 400–500 words.

Explain causes of both crisis and fall, not merely narrate emperors. The following are research dimensions, not extra compulsory scoring aspects.

aspects.name: Research dimension: social conflict

facts.claim: Appian describes agrarian conflict, the veto/removal of Octavius, and the violent death of Tiberius Gracchus.

aspects.causal_explanation: Evaluator inference: Link distributional pressures, reform conflict and erosion of peaceful norms; do not assume one reform alone caused the entire collapse.

aspects.name: Research dimension: competition and military power

facts.claim: Plutarch describes Gallic resources supporting Caesar’s political influence and his crossing of the Rubicon into Italy.

aspects.causal_explanation: Evaluator inference: Explain how personal military resources and disputes about command could overcome institutional compromise and lead to civil war.

aspects.name: Research dimension: settlement and institutional continuity

facts.claim: In Res Gestae 34, Augustus claims restoration to Senate and people while acknowledging pre-eminent authority.

aspects.causal_explanation: Evaluator inference: Distinguish formal Republican language from concentrated leadership; explain a transition rather than assuming every institution vanished overnight.

traps.claim_or_issue: Augustus’ restoration claim proves that competitive Republican government fully returned.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Treat the inscription as political self-presentation and distinguish formal powers from authority.

traps.claim_or_issue: A single date, person or economic factor is the only possible explanation.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Allow a defensible periodization but require mechanisms connecting several relevant developments.

topics.interpretive_flexibility: No mandatory terminal year or single master cause: accept coherent multi-causal arguments and qualified alternatives supported by the chronology.

Facts below are illustrative anchors, not an exhaustive required inventory or a model essay. Accept other independently verified relevant evidence.
Present the genesis and assess consequences for Europe. Religious, political and economic aspects are expressly required.

aspects.name: Religious

facts.claim: Urban II’s Clermont appeal linked aid to Eastern Christians with spiritual remission; his December 1095 letter documents mobilization.
The Fourth Crusade’s sack of Constantinople in 1204 intensified estrangement between Byzantine and Western Christians.

aspects.causal_explanation: Evaluator inference: religious authority and spiritual reward motivated participation; later conflict within Christianity damaged solidarity. Do not claim the Christian schism began in 1204 or all participants had identical motives.

aspects.name: Political

facts.claim: The Fourth Crusade diverted to Constantinople, sacked in 1204; a Latin Empire was established.

aspects.causal_explanation: Evaluator inference: Relate armed intervention to changed authority and damaged relations between Western and Byzantine Christians; avoid treating every expedition as the same conflict.

aspects.name: Economic

facts.claim: The Met cites Ibn Jubayr’s 1183–1185 observation of trade through Frankish and Muslim territories despite hostilities.

aspects.causal_explanation: Evaluator inference: Discuss commercial contact and wartime exchange as a qualified economic consequence; trade coexisted with war and was not created from nothing by crusading.

traps.claim_or_issue: Every crusade targeted Muslims in Jerusalem, or all crusaders sought only land.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Targets and motives varied; Constantinople and spiritual mobilization contradict these universal claims.

traps.claim_or_issue: Crusades alone created European commerce or necessarily enriched all Europeans.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Specify a mechanism and beneficiaries; evidence of exchange does not prove a single cause or universal prosperity.

traps.claim_or_issue: Reported Clermont speeches are exact contemporary transcripts.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Compare later narrative versions with the papal letter; accept the broad mobilization evidence without requiring verbatim words.

topics.interpretive_flexibility: Accept mixed or primarily negative/positive assessments with specified European consequences; causal links must not substitute an unsupported universal verdict for evidence.

Characterize the course of the First Crusade. The dimensions organize chronology and mechanisms; no extra compulsory scoring aspects are named.

aspects.name: Research dimension: mobilization

facts.claim: Urban II promoted the expedition at Clermont in 1095 and followed with a December letter of instruction.

aspects.causal_explanation: Evaluator inference: Connect religious summons and organization to the formation of an expedition rather than starting without its mobilization.

aspects.name: Research dimension: campaign and siege

facts.claim: Anselm’s February 1098 letter reports Nicaea’s capture before the ongoing Antioch siege; his July letter reports Antioch’s capture.
Stephen’s March 1098 letter describes winter, supply shortages and fighting at Antioch.

aspects.causal_explanation: Evaluator inference: Use ordered stages and concrete logistical or military difficulties to explain progress; the sources’ triumphal numbers are not reliable exact counts.

aspects.name: Research dimension: Jerusalem and outcome

facts.claim: Jerusalem fell on 15 July 1099 after a siege; eyewitness accounts describe mass killing.
The collected accounts describe siege preparations and Frankish violence after capture.

aspects.causal_explanation: Evaluator inference: Explain how capture completed the principal goal while acknowledging violence and the creation of new territorial obligations.

traps.claim_or_issue: Constantinople’s sack in 1204 was an event of the First Crusade.
Chronicle enemy numbers or blood-depth imagery are precise measurements.
traps.correction_or_caveat: These are rhetorically charged participant narratives, not modern statistical records.

topics.interpretive_flexibility: Accept selective but coherent major-stage narration and other verified campaign anchors; do not demand every battle or an exact thesis about success.

Present causes and course in fourteenth-century Europe and assess consequences. Demographic, social and economic aspects are expressly required. Separate modern causation from contemporary beliefs.

aspects.name: Demographic

facts.claim: The Nature study dates the Black Death to 1347–1351, providing the epidemic’s bounded course beyond the local 1348 cases.
Ancient DNA identifies Yersinia pestis in London Black Death victims of 1348–1350.
The archival overview places the plague in Britain in 1348.
Modern plague biology identifies infected fleas and animals as transmission routes.

aspects.causal_explanation: Evaluator inference: Relate infection and movement/contact to mortality and spread; distinguish a demonstrated pathogen from an unsupported unique route or uniform mortality percentage.

aspects.name: Social

facts.claim: Boccaccio describes disrupted households and hurried funeral practices in Florence in 1348.

aspects.causal_explanation: Evaluator inference: Explain how mass illness and death strained care and customary social obligations; a city account is evidence of disruption, not proof of identical behaviour everywhere.

aspects.name: Economic

facts.claim: The English Statute of Labourers of 1351 sought to constrain wages after labour shortages; it followed the 1349 ordinance.

aspects.causal_explanation: Evaluator inference: Connect mortality to labour scarcity, bargaining and attempted elite/state control. Specify location and avoid an instantaneous Europe-wide end of serfdom.

traps.claim_or_issue: Celestial influence or divine anger is the demonstrated biological cause.
traps.correction_or_caveat: These were contemporary explanations, distinct from modern pathogen evidence.

traps.claim_or_issue: Exactly the same fraction died everywhere or serfdom immediately ended throughout Europe.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Regional and class variation matter; the English wage-control response supports a narrower mechanism.

topics.interpretive_flexibility: Accept different supported assessments of class, regional and long-term effects. Exact aggregate mortality estimates are not mandatory; causes and course still require explicit treatment.

requirements: Choose one alternative; state and justify a position with historical evidence; requested length 400–500 words.

Explain contemporary interpretations and reactions. The following dimensions are research aids, not added compulsory scoring aspects.

aspects.name: Research dimension: beliefs

facts.claim: Boccaccio reports celestial influence/divine anger explanations and fragrant substances used against feared bad air.

aspects.causal_explanation: Evaluator inference: Show how explanatory frameworks informed action without requiring medieval people to know germ theory.

aspects.name: Research dimension: individual and collective responses

facts.claim: Florentine responses included isolation, flight, drinking, cleaning measures, exclusion of the sick and religious processions.
facts.locator: Public measures and different modes of living

aspects.causal_explanation: Evaluator inference: Compare different attempts to manage risk or distress, rather than asserting a single universal response.

aspects.name: Research dimension: regulation

facts.claim: English authorities adopted wage regulation in the Statute of Labourers in 1351.

aspects.causal_explanation: Evaluator inference: A response could address social/economic consequences as well as disease itself; connect regulation to perceived disorder and labour scarcity.

traps.claim_or_issue: All responses were identical, or every action was merely irrational.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Distinguish observed precautions, social regulation and religious meaning; evidence of belief is not proof of effectiveness.

traps.claim_or_issue: Modern pathogen knowledge is attributed to fourteenth-century observers.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Present scientific causation as retrospective knowledge and contemporary explanations as beliefs.

topics.interpretive_flexibility: Accept other verified beliefs, persecutory actions, charitable responses or local ordinances. Do not require examples absent from this non-exhaustive shortlist.
